analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal subsidies, tax breaks, and liability caps for oil, gas, and coal companies.
analysis.headline: The bill got no cosponsors and no committee action; it died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended an estimated range of federal support for fossil fuel production: royalty relief on offshore oil and gas leases, higher minimum royalties for coal and oil on federal land, repeal of a federal research office for fossil energy, a ban on using World Bank, Export-Import Bank, and overseas investment funds for fossil projects, an end to more than a dozen tax breaks for oil, gas, and coal producers, a new 13% tax on crude oil and natural gas taken from the Gulf of Mexico seabed, and removal of the cap on oil companies' liability for offshore spills. It was introduced by one senator, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would stop paying for royalty relief, tax breaks, research funding, loan guarantees, and international financing that support fossil fuel companies; communities near offshore drilling and pipelines, who would benefit from uncapped spill liability and a larger Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund; and federal treasuries in coal and energy-producing states, since the bill nearly doubles minimum royalties on federal coal and oil leases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near fossil fuel operations

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the Interior Department's authority to grant royalty relief on Outer Continental Shelf oil and gas leases and repeals Energy Policy Act incentives for deep and shallow-water Gulf production, so companies pay full value for publicly owned resources [S2] [S3].
Raises the minimum royalty on federal coal, oil, and natural gas leases from 12.5% to 18.75%, increasing what companies pay to extract public resources [S3].

Removes the $75 million cap above insurance requirements on offshore facility and pipeline operators' spill liability and extends full liability to pipelines carrying diluted bitumen, so taxpayers are less likely to absorb cleanup costs [S3].

Terminates the Office of Fossil Energy Research and Development, repeals the ultra-deepwater and unconventional petroleum research program, and bars federal loan guarantees for advanced fossil energy and refinery projects [S2] [S3].

Prohibits World Bank, Export-Import Bank, Overseas Private Investment Corporation, and Department of Energy advanced-research funds from financing fossil fuel projects, and rescinds unobligated balances for that purpose [S2] [S3].

Repeals or limits more than a dozen tax provisions benefiting oil, gas, and coal producers — including enhanced oil recovery credits, percentage depletion, intangible drilling cost deductions, the domestic manufacturing deduction for fossil and hard mineral production, and last-in-first-out accounting for fossil companies [S3].

Imposes a 13% tax on crude oil and natural gas removed from the Gulf of Mexico outer continental shelf, creditable against federal royalties paid, and bars tax deductions for oil spill removal costs and damages [S3].
Blocks Department of Transportation grants and loans for rail or port projects that transport fossil fuel and bars Rural Electrification Act loans for fossil fuel projects [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies, which would lose royalty relief, preferential tax treatment, federal research and loan-guarantee support, and their capped spill liability. Some of those costs — particularly the royalty increases, the 13% Gulf severance tax, and the higher per-barrel Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund rate — could be passed through to consumers in the form of somewhat higher fuel and electricity prices, and higher royalty rates could make some federal leasing uneconomic, reducing production and the state and local revenue tied to it.

drawbacks.text: Higher royalties, the 13% Gulf severance tax, and the repeal of tax preferences would raise companies' production costs, some portion of which would likely reach consumers as higher fuel, heating, and electricity prices [S3].

Raising the federal coal royalty from 12.5% to 18.75% and designating the Powder River Basin for a fair-market-value study could make Powder River Basin coal uneconomic, threatening jobs and tax revenue in Montana and Wyoming communities that depend on it [S3].
Repealing the domestic manufacturing deduction for hard mineral mining reaches mining of any hard mineral, not only fossil fuels, so non-fossil mining operations would lose that deduction too [S3].
Ending fossil-fuel research programs and loan guarantees with no replacement funding leaves fossil-dependent regions and workers with no federal transition assistance in the bill [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but lopsided: the bill recaptures public money and public risk that currently go to highly profitable energy companies, and the largest costs fall on those companies rather than on the public. The honest costs are that some portion of the new royalties and taxes would show up in energy prices, and that coal-dependent communities in the Powder River Basin would bear a disproportionate share of the adjustment with no transition help in the bill. On balance the benefits to taxpayers and spill-exposed communities outweigh the costs, though the bill's breadth — touching everything from tax accounting rules to rail grants — would have required careful implementation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the End Polluter Welfare Act of 2013 on November 21, 2013 [S5] [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].

The bill's own findings noted the oil and gas industry spent $105 million on lobbying in the first three quarters of 2013 and had received over $72 billion in federal fossil fuel subsidies from 2002 to 2008 [S3].
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill still sitting in committee, so all its provisions expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal companies are better off: they kept the royalty relief, tax preferences, federal research funding, loan-guarantee eligibility, and capped spill liability the bill would have removed, at no cost.

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor; it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, of which he is not a member, the day it was introduced.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral: no markup, no hearing on the bill in the record, and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded; the bill had a single independent sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so the parties never had to take a position on the record.

industries.note: The bill strips royalty relief on Gulf leases, repeals more than a dozen tax preferences including percentage depletion and intangible drilling cost deductions, ends domestic manufacturing and LIFO accounting benefits, and adds a 13% severance tax on Gulf production. These companies currently extract public resources on terms that shift public money and spill risk to taxpayers, which is exactly what the bill would have ended.

industries.industry: Coal producers, especially in the Powder River Basin
industries.note: Minimum federal royalties would rise from 12.5% to 18.75%, coal percentage depletion and capital gains treatment for coal royalties would end, and the Powder River Basin would get a fair-market-value royalty study. Coal mined from public land at below-market rates transfers public wealth to leaseholders.

The $75 million liability cap above insurance would be removed and extended to bitumen pipelines, and spill removal costs would no longer be tax-deductible. The current cap leaves taxpayers exposed to cleanup costs above the limit, as the 2010 Gulf spill demonstrated.

industries.industry: Export credit and international financing institutions (Export-Import Bank, OPIC, World Bank fossil lending)
industries.note: Federal money and loan guarantees would be barred from supporting fossil fuel projects abroad, ending a channel through which U.S. taxpayers back overseas fossil infrastructure.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel transport (rail and port operators handling coal and oil)
industries.note: Department of Transportation grants and loans could no longer fund rail or port projects that move fossil fuel, ending public support for fossil logistics infrastructure.
